title: Der Fuchs und das Pferd
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 132. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, Thür, Rath, that, thun).
about: KHM 132 is short and brisk: a farmer turns out his old horse to fend for itself once it can no longer work, and the horse, in despair, is talked by a fox into a trick — luring a lion into a trap by pretending it can only be tied down with the horse's own tail — that wins it a home for the rest of its days.

sentences.t: Es hatte ein Bauer ein treues Pferd, das war alt geworden und konnte keine Dienste mehr thun,
sentences.l: A farmer had a faithful horse, that had grown old and could do no services any more,
sentences.i: A farmer had a faithful horse that had grown old and could no longer do any work,
sentences.n: The dummy “es” opens the sentence again (“Es hatte ein Bauer …”), a standing way of beginning a tale. “Dienste thun” is to render service, said of a servant or a working animal; “thun” is the 1857 spelling of tun. Das Pferd is neuter, so the German calls the horse “es” all the way through, and so does the literal line.

sentences.t: da wollte ihm sein Herr nichts mehr zu fressen geben und sprach „brauchen kann ich dich freilich nicht mehr, indeß mein ich es gut mit dir,
sentences.l: so its master would give it nothing more to eat and said, “use you I certainly cannot any more, however I mean well by you,
sentences.i: so its master would give it nothing more to eat, and said, “I can certainly make no more use of you; still, I mean you well;
sentences.n: “fressen” is the verb for an animal’s eating, against Essen for people; the tale uses it of the horse here and again in its very last line. “indeß” is not ‘meanwhile’ here but ‘however, all the same’ (1857 spelling of indes). “mein” is the verb meinen, ‘I mean,’ not the possessive. Fronting the object — “brauchen kann ich dich …” — throws the weight onto the uselessness.

sentences.t: zeigst du dich noch so stark, daß du mir einen Löwen hierher bringst, so will ich dich behalten, jetzt aber mach dich fort aus meinem Stall,“ und jagte es damit ins weite Feld.
sentences.l: if you show yourself still so strong that you bring me a lion here, then I will keep you; but now take yourself off out of my stable,” and with that drove it into the wide field.
sentences.i: if you can show yourself still strong enough to bring me a lion here, then I will keep you; but for now, be off out of my stable,” and with that he drove it out into the open country.
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn once more: the verb comes first (“zeigst du dich …, so will ich …”) and the answering “so” marks the result clause. “noch so stark, daß” is ‘still strong enough that.’ “sich fortmachen” is to take oneself off. Turning a worn-out animal loose “ins weite Feld” is what the first line has been leading to.

sentences.t: Das Pferd war traurig und gieng nach dem Wald zu, dort ein wenig Schutz vor dem Wetter zu suchen.
sentences.l: The horse was sad and went toward the forest, to seek there a little shelter from the weather.
sentences.i: The horse was downcast and made for the forest, to look for a little shelter there from the weather.
sentences.n: “nach dem Wald zu” — the trailing “zu” reinforces the direction, ‘off toward the forest.’ “dort … zu suchen” is a bare infinitive of purpose where modern German would more often write “um … zu suchen.”

sentences.t: Da begegnete ihm der Fuchs und sprach „was hängst du so den Kopf und gehst so einsam herum?“
sentences.l: There the fox met it and said, “why do you hang your head so and go about so alone?”
sentences.i: There the fox came upon it and said, “why do you hang your head like that, and go about so alone?”
sentences.n: “begegnen” takes the dative rather than an object — literally ‘there to it the fox met.’ “was” stands here for “warum,” ‘why,’ an old usage very common in these tales. “den Kopf hängen” is exactly the English ‘to hang one’s head.’

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete das Pferd, „Geiz und Treue wohnen nicht beisammen in einem Haus:
sentences.l: “Ah,” answered the horse, “greed and loyalty do not dwell together in one house:
sentences.i: “Ah,” answered the horse, “avarice and loyalty do not live under one roof:
sentences.n: “Treue” is the noun, die Treue, loyalty — not the adjective treu with which the horse was described in the opening line. German lets the reader hear the connection, and the whole tale turns on it. The line has the shape of a proverb, and the horse delivers it as one.

sentences.t: mein Herr hat vergessen was ich ihm für Dienste in so vielen Jahren geleistet habe, und weil ich nicht recht mehr ackern kann, will er mir kein Futter mehr geben, und hat mich fortgejagt.“
sentences.l: my master has forgotten what services I have rendered him in so many years, and because I can no longer plough properly, he will give me no more fodder, and has driven me away.”
sentences.i: my master has forgotten what services I rendered him over so many years, and because I can no longer plough as I should, he will give me no more fodder, and has driven me off.”
sentences.n: “was ich ihm für Dienste … geleistet habe” splits the pair “was für” — ‘what sort of services’ — around the rest of the clause, something English cannot imitate. “Dienste leisten” is to render service. “nicht recht” is ‘not properly, not as one should.’

sentences.t: „Ohne allen Trost?“ fragte der Fuchs.
sentences.l: “With no comfort at all?” asked the fox.
sentences.n: “ohne allen Trost” — “allen” strengthens it to ‘without any comfort whatever.’ The fox is asking whether the master really turned it out with nothing, not even a kind word; the answer is going to be that the comfort offered was worse than none.

sentences.t: „Der Trost war schlecht, er hat gesagt wenn ich noch so stark wäre, daß ich ihm einen Löwen brächte, wollt er mich behalten, aber er weiß wohl, daß ich das nicht vermag.“
sentences.l: “The comfort was poor: he said if I were still so strong that I brought him a lion, he would keep me, but he knows well that I cannot do it.”
sentences.i: “The comfort was a poor one; he said that if I were still strong enough to bring him a lion he would keep me — but he knows perfectly well that I am not able to.”
sentences.n: “weiß” here is the verb wissen, ‘knows,’ not the adjective weiß, ‘white’ — a spelling that answers to two quite different words. “wäre” and “brächte” are subjunctives, the ordinary German way of reporting what someone else said. “vermögen” is a more formal ‘to be able,’ and the horse’s reaching for it is a touch of dignity.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs sprach „da will ich dir helfen, leg dich nur hin, strecke dich aus und rege dich nicht, als wärst du todt.“
sentences.l: The fox said, “then I will help you: just lie yourself down, stretch yourself out and do not stir, as if you were dead.”
sentences.i: The fox said, “then I will help you: just lie down, stretch yourself out and do not stir, as though you were dead.”
sentences.n: Three commands in a row, all reflexive or separable — “leg dich hin,” “strecke dich aus,” “rege dich nicht” — of which English keeps only ‘stretch yourself out.’ “rege” is from sich regen, ‘to stir,’ a verb here and not the adjective rege. “nur” softens the imperative to ‘just.’

sentences.t: Das Pferd that was der Fuchs verlangte,
sentences.l: The horse did what the fox demanded,
sentences.n: “that” is once more the 1857 spelling of tat. There is no relative pronoun: “was” alone does the work of ‘that which.’

sentences.t: der Fuchs aber gieng zum Löwen, der seine Höhle nicht weit davon hatte und sprach „da draußen liegt ein todtes Pferd, komm doch mit hinaus, da kannst du eine fette Mahlzeit halten.“
sentences.l: but the fox went to the lion, who had his cave not far from there, and said, “out there lies a dead horse; do come out along, there you can have a fat meal.”
sentences.i: but the fox went off to the lion, whose den was not far from the spot, and said, “there is a dead horse lying out there; do come out with me, and you can make a rich meal of it.”
sentences.n: “eine Mahlzeit halten” is to take a meal. “komm doch mit hinaus” stacks two particles on one imperative — “mit,” along with me, and “hinaus,” out there — which English has to unpack into a phrase. “todtes” keeps the 1857 -th- (modern totes).

sentences.t: Der Löwe gieng mit und wie sie bei dem Pferd standen, sprach der Fuchs „hier hast dus doch nicht nach deiner Gemächlichkeit, weißt du was?
sentences.l: The lion went along, and as they stood by the horse, the fox said, “here you have it not at all to your comfort — do you know what?
sentences.i: The lion went along, and when they were standing over the horse the fox said, “you have it here in no comfort at all — do you know what?
sentences.n: Gemächlichkeit is unhurried ease; ‘not to your comfort’ means the lion cannot eat at leisure out in the open. “dus” is du + es run together, a spoken contraction the 1857 text prints as it sounds. “weißt du was?” is the everyday opening of a proposal, ‘tell you what.’

sentences.t: ich wills mit dem Schweif an dich binden, so kannst dus in deine Höhle ziehen und in aller Ruhe verzehren.“
sentences.l: I will bind it to you by the tail, then you can drag it into your den and eat it up in all quiet.”
sentences.i: I will tie it to you by the tail, and then you can drag it into your den and eat it at your leisure.”
sentences.n: “wills” and “dus” are more of the same clipped speech (will es, du es). “in aller Ruhe” is ‘in perfect peace, at leisure’ — the fox is offering exactly the comfort he has just said was missing, and that offer is the trap.

sentences.t: Dem Löwen gefiel der Rath, er stellte sich hin und damit ihm der Fuchs das Pferd festknüpfen könnte, hielt er ganz still.
sentences.l: The counsel pleased the lion; he placed himself there, and so that the fox could knot the horse fast to him, he held quite still.
sentences.i: The lion liked the plan; he took his stand, and so that the fox could tie the horse fast to him, he held perfectly still.
sentences.n: “gefallen” takes the dative of the person pleased: “dem Löwen gefiel der Rath” is ‘the counsel pleased the lion,’ where English prefers ‘the lion liked it.’ “Rath” is the 1857 spelling of Rat, counsel. “damit … könnte” is a purpose clause, ‘so that he might.’

sentences.t: Der Fuchs aber band mit des Pferdes Schweif dem Löwen die Beine zusammen und drehte und schnürte alles so wohl und stark, daß es mit keiner Kraft zu zerreißen war.
sentences.l: But the fox bound the lion’s legs together with the horse’s tail and twisted and laced it all so well and strongly that it was not to be torn apart by any strength.
sentences.i: But the fox tied the lion’s legs together with the horse’s tail, and twisted and laced it all so firmly that no strength could have torn it apart.
sentences.n: “band” is the preterite of binden, ‘bound’ — not the noun das Band. “dem Löwen die Beine” is the dative of possession again: ‘the legs to the lion,’ i.e. the lion’s legs. “zu zerreißen war” is the sein + zu construction, which carries the sense ‘could be torn.’

sentences.t: Als er nun sein Werk vollendet hatte, klopfte er dem Pferd auf die Schulter und sprach „zieh, Schimmel, zieh.“
sentences.l: When he had now completed his work, he clapped the horse on the shoulder and said, “pull, Schimmel, pull.”
sentences.i: When he had finished his work he clapped the horse on the shoulder and said, “pull, grey, pull.”
sentences.n: “dem Pferd auf die Schulter klopfen” splits the whole from the part: dative for the horse, accusative for the shoulder. “Schimmel” is the word for a white or grey horse and is used here the way a name would be, as a carter would call to his own animal; the literal line keeps the German word, the idiomatic one turns it into ‘grey.’

sentences.t: Da sprang das Pferd mit einmal auf und zog den Löwen mit sich fort.
sentences.l: Then the horse sprang up all at once and drew the lion away with it.
sentences.i: Then the horse sprang up all at once and dragged the lion off with it.
sentences.n: “mit einmal” is ‘all at once, in a single movement’ (modern mit einem Mal). “sprang … auf” and “zog … fort” are both separable, and both particles wait at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Der Löwe fieng an zu brüllen, daß die Vögel in dem ganzen Wald vor Schrecken aufflogen, aber das Pferd ließ ihn brüllen, zog und schleppte ihn über das Feld vor seines Herrn Thür.
sentences.l: The lion began to roar, so that the birds in the whole forest flew up in fright, but the horse let him roar, drew and dragged him across the field to its master’s door.
sentences.i: The lion set up such a roaring that the birds in the whole forest flew up in terror; but the horse let him roar, and hauled and dragged him across the field to its master’s door.
sentences.n: “fieng an” is the 1857 spelling of fing an, from separable anfangen. “daß” here introduces a result, ‘so that.’ “vor Schrecken” uses the vor of cause, ‘out of fright.’ “seines Herrn Thür” puts the genitive in front of its noun, an elevated older order (modern: die Thür seines Herrn).

sentences.t: Wie der Herr das sah, besann er sich eines bessern und sprach zu dem Pferd, „du sollst bei mir bleiben und es gut haben,“ und gab ihm satt zu fressen bis es starb.
sentences.l: When the master saw that, he thought better of it and said to the horse, “you shall stay with me and have it good,” and gave it enough to eat until it died.
sentences.i: When the master saw that, he thought better of it and said to the horse, “you shall stay with me and be well kept,” and gave it its fill to eat until it died.
sentences.n: “sich eines bessern besinnen” is a fixed phrase governing a genitive — to bethink oneself of something better, i.e. to change one’s mind. “es gut haben” is ‘to be well off.’ The last words return to fressen, the animal-eating verb the master used in refusing it in the first place.

glossary.band: binden — bound, tied (3rd sg. preterite; zusammenbinden: to tie together); also das Band, a band or ribbon
glossary.bessern: besser — better (inflected; sich eines bessern besinnen: to think better of it, change one’s mind)
glossary.es: es — it (the horse, das Pferd being neuter, which is how the tale names it throughout); also the dummy subject, Es hatte ein Bauer …
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, to it (dative; used both of the horse, neuter, and of its master)
glossary.indeß: indeß — however, all the same (1857 spelling of indes; also ‘meanwhile’)
glossary.klopfte: klopfen — patted, clapped (3rd sg. preterite; jemandem auf die Schulter klopfen: to clap someone on the shoulder); also ‘knocked’
glossary.leg: hinlegen — lie down (2nd sg. imperative: leg dich … hin, separable hin-); legen alone: to lay, to put
glossary.mein: meinen — mean, think (1st sg. present, short for meine; ich mein es gut mit dir: I mean well by you); also mein, ‘my’
glossary.rege: sich regen — stir, move (2nd sg. imperative: rege dich nicht, do not stir); also the adjective rege, ‘astir, active’
glossary.strecke: ausstrecken — stretch out (2nd sg. imperative: strecke dich aus; separable aus-); also die Strecke, a stretch or distance
glossary.treue: die Treue — loyalty, faithfulness (noun); also treue, the inflected adjective treu ‘faithful’
glossary.weiß: wissen — know (1st/3rd sg. present: ich weiß, er weiß); also weiß, the adjective ‘white’
glossary.wollt: wollen — would, wanted to (3rd sg. preterite, clipped wollte: wollt er mich behalten); also wollt, the 2nd pl. ‘you want’
